settingText: Present-day Tyrellis Vault district, an old civic quarter whose museums display unidentified objects from a past everyone assumes is remote.
summary: The trio follows a catalog trail from the Vael-Tor records to Tyrellis, where an object labeled as remote antiquity turns out to be Theo's own attaché satchel. The discovery converts their missing personal choices into a chronology problem the present world cannot explain.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Establish the Tyrellis museum with the Vael-Tor catalog cross-reference still open on Rae's paper notes. That trail brought them here; school visitors and ordinary staff continue around them while Theo stops at one small plain display case.

Panel 2 — Close on the worn attaché satchel behind glass. Theo says, 'That's mine.' Nothing glows or activates; recognition comes from scratches, softened corners and a clasp that sits slightly wrong.

Panel 3 — Rae asks, 'You're sure?' Theo answers, 'The clasp sticks on the left.' His hand is already held in the old opening grip beside the display case, thumb angled toward the left-side clasp; he notices his own hand and goes still.

Panel 4 — Adrian says only, 'Theo.' Theo turns toward the museum label and asks how old the sign says it is. Adrian's discomfort is interpersonal, not technical. Adrian: 'Don't read the sign.' End with Theo already reading it while his remembered ownership and the institution's confident false interpretation occupy the same quiet frame.

dialogueInline.text: The clasp sticks on the left.
How old does the sign say it is?

summary: Flux debuts over a cup of something going cold while Afterlight asks why everyone keeps demanding answers from someone who has spent the war learning how many answers can be wrong.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Ancient Tyrellis waystation kitchen late in the day. A cup has gone cold beside Flux. Afterlight finds them still sitting where others left them hours ago. Keep the room small, practical and tired.

Panel 2 — Afterlight stands in the kitchen doorway with one shoulder against the frame. Flux remains seated at the table beside the cold cup, coat still on, gaze fixed on the closed council-room door. 'They're waiting for you.' / 'They've been waiting for me since breakfast.'
Panel 3 — Afterlight notes that it is nearly dark. Flux answers, 'Then they're improving.' Give the joke a thin edge; exhaustion is visible underneath it.
Panel 4 — Afterlight: 'Mero needs an answer.' Flux looks toward the closed door where the decision-makers are waiting, but does not rise.
Panel 5 — Flux: 'Mero needs permission. That's different.' Afterlight looks from Flux to the closed council-room door, then pulls out the chair opposite him and sits instead of urging him toward it.

dialogueInline.text: They've been waiting for me since breakfast.
Mero wants me to bless the answer he already likes.

summary: Rae finds one of her ancient annotations bound into a later civic record. Successive generations of apparent history have treated her handwriting as anonymous source material. The physical chain is too continuous to feel like remote antiquity.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Rae and Theo in the municipal archive beneath the museum. Paper, reused bindings and ordinary clerical wear dominate; avoid futuristic data-display spectacle. Rae pauses over a later civic volume and says, 'This is mine.' Theo assumes she means the handwriting.
Panel 2 — Insert on one tiny correction in the margin, physically incorporated into a later binding. Rae: 'The correction.' The evidence is mundane enough to be harder to dismiss.

Panel 3 — Theo: 'That's worse somehow.' Rae lays two reused records side by side and traces matching physical repairs, handwriting and ownership marks across them; no hidden screen or archive mechanism appears.

Panel 4 — Rae: 'Because nobody preserved it. They just kept using it.' End tight on layers of old paper: erased headings, later annotations, patched tears and fresh present-day handling marks occupying the same sheets.

dialogueInline.text: Because nobody preserved it. They just kept using it.

summary: Mero asks Flux which choice survives. Flux hears the request as an attempt to move responsibility into the future.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Ancient council room after the argument has emptied out. Chairs stand crooked around abandoned papers; Mero remains at the table and Flux is the only other person still in the room.
Panel 2 — Medium two-shot across the abandoned council table.
Panel 3 — Mero leans forward with both palms on scattered papers: 'Tell me which choice survives.' Flux looks from the papers to Mero's face, then folds one sheet closed before answering.
Panel 4 — Flux: 'You mean which choice lets you sleep.' Mero: 'I haven't slept in months.' Keep both exhausted, not theatrical.

dialogueInline.text: Tell me which one doesn't make this worse.
You mean which choice lets you sleep.

summary: Flux refuses to certify Mero's decision and makes him own the choice himself.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Flux tells Mero, 'Then stop asking me to make the decision feel safer.' Mero grips the back of an empty chair.
Panel 2 — Mero's knuckles whiten; he releases the chair and steps away instead of answering immediately.
Panel 3 — Mero looks at the folded projections and says, 'I need something.'
Panel 4 — Flux answers, 'I'm not signing it for you. Pick one and call it yours.'
Panel 5 — Flux pushes the folded paper back across the table and leaves Mero standing among the empty chairs.

settingText: Present-day stairwell beneath Tyrellis archive, old stone continuing seamlessly into modern construction.
summary: Theo asks whether he woke up thousands of years after the war. Adrian finally tells him that the question assumes a clean gap that the Reset did not leave behind.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Theo and Adrian descend an ordinary stairwell where ancient stone continues into modern repairs with no clean boundary. Theo asks, 'How much time is missing?'
Panel 2 — Adrian: 'That's not what was removed.' He keeps descending the stairs while Theo and Rae stop above him. Adrian does not turn toward the museum labels or offer any visual aid.

Panel 3 — Theo stops on the stairs and points upward toward the museum level: 'Then why does everything call us ancient?' Keep the old lower stone courses and newer upper masonry visible in the same vertical frame. Adrian: 'Because the world needed a story that connected yesterday to today.' Theo: 'And it made one up?'

Panel 4 — Adrian stops on a landing where dark ancient stone continues directly into pale modern repair with matching worn stair edges: 'It healed around the wound.' Theo stands one step below him, looking at the continuous masonry instead of Adrian.

dialogueInline.text: Then why does everything call us ancient?
Because people needed a history that connected yesterday to today.
The gap filled in. Records, families, institutions—everything kept going.

settingText: Ancient Tyrellis balcony overlooking refugee routes at dusk.
summary: Starbreaker asks Flux whether decisive action will prevent the catastrophe he fears. Flux refuses to bless the choice. Starbreaker accuses Flux of hiding behind uncertainty; Flux says certainty has become the most dangerous weapon in the room.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Ancient balcony at dusk above refugee movement. Flux and Starbreaker stand apart from the traffic below; keep the human evacuation legible so their argument has people attached to it.
Panel 2 — Starbreaker: 'You've seen what happens if I wait.' Flux: 'I've seen what happens if you don't.' Neither future is visualized as a clean prophetic diagram.

Panel 3 — Starbreaker closes the distance until he and Flux are nearly face-to-face: 'So pick one.' Flux stays against the balcony rail, hands open and empty: 'That's your job.' Refugees continue moving below them.
Panel 4 — Starbreaker: 'Coward.' Let Flux absorb it; for a beat they are unsure whether he is wrong.
Panel 5 — Flux: 'Maybe. But I won't turn fear into permission for you.' End with Starbreaker looking back toward the people whose fate he still has to choose about.

dialogueInline.text: You've seen what happens if I wait.
I've seen what happens if you don't.
Maybe. I'm still not giving you permission.

settingText: Present-day Tyrellis street market above the archive, ordinary evening traffic continuing around ancient foundations.
summary: Theo and Rae step into an ordinary Tyrellis market while messages from Vark and Calum remind them that the memory crisis is already altering jobs, records and institutions. Their argument about disclosure is grounded in people whose present lives are being changed without explanation.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Theo and Rae emerge into the ordinary evening market above the archive. Vendors close stalls, families carry groceries, workers change shifts. Theo listens to a short voice note from Vark while walking: Sector Four remains closed and Vark's crew has been reassigned without an explanation anyone believes.

Panel 2 — Rae reads a terse message from Calum while helping a vendor pick up dropped papers: Zenith has quietly pulled three more returning records from public access, but Calum sent Rae the titles before they disappeared. His help remains cautious and institutionally compromised rather than a full change of allegiance.

Panel 3 — Theo pockets the message device: 'They're living on a lie.' Rae watches a family arguing over dinner money while one parent checks a work schedule: 'They're living.' Theo asks, 'So we say nothing?' Rae answers, 'We say nothing we can't take back.'

Panel 4 — Theo: 'You don't get to decide when they're ready.' Rae: 'Neither do you.' End on the market continuing around them: current jobs, errands, families and obligations remain real even while hidden history presses underneath them.

dialogueInline.text: Vark: Sector Four's still closed. They moved my crew to Nine. Nobody will say why.
Calum: Zenith pulled three more returning records this morning. I sent the titles before someone else decides what they mean.
We say nothing we can't take back.
You don't get to decide when they're ready.

summary: Afterlight finds Flux preparing to leave. Flux says everyone now hears only the future they want from them. Afterlight asks where Flux will go; Flux genuinely does not know.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Return to the ancient kitchen late at night. Flux packs one small bag on the chair. The same cold cup from the morning remains untouched on the table beside a dried ring of spilled drink.

Panel 2 — Afterlight: 'You're leaving.' Flux: 'I'm trying.' Afterlight steps sideways out of the doorway and leaves a clear path to the hall; her hands stay at her sides. Afterlight: 'Where?' Flux stops with one hand on the doorframe and the packed bag hanging from the other. He stares into the empty corridor before answering.

Panel 3 — Flux stands with the small packed bag in hand at the open doorway: 'Somewhere nobody asks me what happens next.' Afterlight remains beside the table and cold cup: 'That place doesn't exist.' Neither moves toward the other.
Panel 4 — Flux: 'Then maybe I'll finally be surprised.' End on the cold cup and the open doorway after Flux moves toward it; do not imply where they go or foreshadow a technical explanation.

dialogueInline.text: Somewhere nobody asks me what happens next.
Then maybe I'll finally be surprised.

summary: Adrian admits the Reset did not create a false universe by design. It removed meaning so comprehensively that institutions, stories and ordinary lives settled around the absence. He cannot tell where scar tissue ends and authentic post-Reset history begins.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Archive after closing. Adrian finally sits at an ordinary table with Rae and Theo instead of pacing away from the question.

Panel 2 — Rae: 'Which parts are real?' Adrian answers, 'All of them.' Keep all three at the physical table with books and records between them; Rae presses one palm onto the open pages while Adrian meets her eyes.
Panel 3 — Theo: 'That's useless.' Adrian: 'It's also true.' The argument stays between people.
Panel 4 — Rae: 'You don't know where the seam is.' Adrian looks at reused records, repaired walls and the two present people in front of him.

Panel 5 — Adrian: 'I don't think there is one seam.' End in a wide table shot: Rae has two reused volumes open, Theo holds a repaired document, and behind Adrian an old wall patch disappears into newer masonry with no clean dividing line.

dialogueInline.text: You don't know where the seam is.
I don't think there's one clean boundary.

summary: Mero comes looking for Flux. The cup from the previous night is still on the table. Flux is gone. There is no message that explains where, why, or whether disappearance was voluntary.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Ancient kitchen the next morning. The same cup is still where Flux left it. Their chair is empty. Nothing is damaged and nothing announces an event. Mero enters looking for Flux and immediately knows something is wrong from Afterlight's face, not from an alarm.

Panel 2 — Mero: 'When did you last see them?' Afterlight: 'Last night.' Keep the empty place visible between them. Mero asks whether Flux said where and whether Afterlight asked. Her answers are simply 'No' and 'Yes.'
Panel 3 — End on the untouched cup, empty chair and ordinary doorway. No portal, residue, body, message or Reset effect. This absence is genuinely unexplained.

dialogueInline.text: When did you last see them?

summary: An ordinary transit worker corrects an erased district name without knowing how he knows it.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — On the ordinary Tyrellis transit platform, a worker pauses mid-announcement and says, 'No. That's not what it was called.'
Panel 2 — Nearby commuters stop walking while the departure flow continues behind them; the worker is startled by their own certainty.
Panel 3 — Rae approaches slowly while the worker tries to repeat the lost place-name and cannot.
Panel 4 — Rae asks, 'What did you call it?' The worker answers, 'I don't know.'
Panel 5 — Rae says, 'You just said you did.' The worker's confusion turns to grief before any historical context arrives.

summary: The transit worker remembers a brother who does not exist in his present biography. His current partner arrives from the same shift and stays with him, making the contradiction a relationship problem rather than an isolated anomaly.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — The transit worker says, 'My brother died there.' Theo asks carefully, 'Do you have a brother?' The worker answers, 'No.' His work radio keeps repeating an ordinary departure call beside him.

Panel 2 — His current partner, still in the same transit-service uniform family but visibly a different person, arrives from farther down the platform after seeing the disruption. Partner: 'You don't have a brother.' Worker: 'I know.' The partner takes the radio from his shaking hand and silences it.

Panel 3 — The worker sits on a service bench and says, 'I miss him.' The partner sits beside him rather than correcting the memory again. Adrian watches from the edge of the platform while commuters continue boarding and station staff quietly cover the worker's shift.
